Empirical Research Plan  
“Large‐scale dams, agricultural productivity and regional development in India, 1970-1999”

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Strategy: Difference-in-Differences (DID) with an event–study extension for staggered adoption.

Why appropriate
•  The policy “treatment” (a new dam becoming operational in a district) is introduced in different places at different years (1970-1999).  
•  We observe multiple pre- and post-treatment years for every district, letting us net out time-invariant district attributes with district FEs and nationwide shocks with year FEs.  
•  Modern staggered-adoption DID estimators (Sun & Abraham 2021; Callaway & Sant’Anna 2021) allow consistent estimation under heterogeneous treatment effects—a likely scenario here.  
•  Event-study coefficients allow us to (i) test the common-trends assumption visually and (ii) trace dynamic effects on agricultural yields, income and poverty.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Treatment variable  
•  Binary: Treated_dt = 1 from the first year t in which at least one dam in district d is completed and remains =1 thereafter.  
•  Intensity (for robustness): #dams_dt or log(storage capacity)_dt.

Control group  
•  Never-treated districts + not-yet-treated districts serve as counterfactuals in each year.

Treatment timing / event date  
•  Event year g_d = first year a dam in district d becomes operational (commissioning date).  
•  Pre-period k<0, post-period k≥0 defined as k = t – g_d.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
--------------------------------------------------------------------
A1. Parallel trends: In the absence of dams, treated and control districts would have followed the same trend in outcomes.  
  • Plausibility: Geographic and political factors guiding dam placement (elevation, river flow) are largely time-invariant and will be absorbed by district FEs. Remaining concern: districts targeted because they were on different growth paths. We will test for pre-trends.

A2. No anticipatory effects: Outcomes do not change before construction because agents foresee the dam.  
  • Plausibility: Long gestation periods make precise anticipation difficult for farmers; pre-trend test will examine this.

A3. Stable unit treatment value (no spillovers across districts).  
  • Plausibility: Large dams can affect downstream irrigation or migration. We will address by (i) excluding districts within 100 km downstream of treated districts in robustness checks, and (ii) clustering standard errors by river-basin × state to allow spatial correlation.

A4. Composition stability: District boundaries/populations stable or appropriately harmonized.  
  • Plausibility: Some district splits occurred; we will harmonize to 1971 boundaries.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Threats to Identification & Mitigation
--------------------------------------------------------------------
T1. Targeted placement based on unobservable growth potential.  
   • Mitigation:  
     – Include district-specific linear trends.  
     – Control for time-varying rainfall, monsoon deviation, and state-specific policy variables.  
     – Instrumental-variable robustness: instrument dam timing with exogenous variation in annual central-government hydropower budget interacted with district‐level hydrological suitability.

T2. Spillovers (downstream or market integration).  
   • Mitigation:  
     – Drop or re-assign neighbouring districts (buffer zones).  
     – Estimate spatial DID with distance weights to measure spillover size directly.

T3. Measurement error in commissioning year.  
   • Mitigation:  
     – Cross-validate commissioning dates with Central Water Commission reports.  
     – Robustness: re-code treatment as “within ±1 year of reported date”.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline
--------------------------------------------------------------------
```r
# 0. Packages -------------------------------------------------------
library(data.table)
library(fixest)          # feols and sunab
library(did)             # Callaway & Sant’Anna
library(ggplot2)

# 1. Load & merge data ---------------------------------------------
dams   <- fread("dams_india_1970_1999.csv")        # dam_id, district, commission_year
agri   <- fread("district_agri_1970_1999.csv")     # district, year, yield, income, poverty
weather<- fread("rainfall_district_1970_1999.csv") # rainfall anomaly, etc.

# Harmonise district codes
setkeyv(dams,   c("district"))
setkeyv(agri,   c("district","year"))
setkeyv(weather,c("district","year"))

# Construct panel
panel <- merge(agri, weather, all.x = TRUE)
# Dam treatment ----------------------------------------------------
firstdam <- dams[ , .(g_year = min(commission_year)), by = district]

panel   <- merge(panel, firstdam, by = "district", all.x=TRUE)
panel[  , treat := (year >= g_year)]
panel[is.na(g_year), treat := 0]      # never treated
panel[  , ever_treated := !is.na(g_year)]

# Event-study timing variable
panel[ever_treated==TRUE, rel_year := year - g_year]
panel[ever_treated==FALSE, rel_year := NA]

# 2. Main DID specification ----------------------------------------
main_eq <- feols(yield ~ sunab(g_year, year) + rainfall + district_trend |
                 district + year,
                 data = panel,
                 cluster = ~district)

summary(main_eq)

# 3. Robustness: Callaway & Sant’Anna ------------------------------
cs <- att_gt(yname  = "yield",
             tname  = "year",
             gname  = "g_year",
             idname = "district",
             xformla= ~ rainfall,
             data   = panel)

agg_effects <- aggte(cs, type = "simple")
summary(agg_effects)

# 4. Placebo pre-trend test ----------------------------------------
pretest <- feols(yield ~ i(rel_year, ref = -1, lag = -10:-1) |
                 district + year,
                 data = panel[abs(rel_year) <= 10])

iplot(pretest) + theme_minimal()
```

--------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Economic theory: Improved irrigation stabilises water supply, raises cropping intensity and allows high-value crops.  
Prior expectations (per dam, within 10 years):  
•  Agricultural yield: +7–10 %.  
•  Average rural income: +4–6 %.  
•  Poverty headcount rate: –2 pp (roughly –8 %).  
Effects likely grow over time (S-shaped adoption) and are larger in arid districts.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (DID)  
(1 = clearly satisfied, 0 = questionable)
C1. No differential pre-trends .................... 0.8  
C2. No anticipation ............................... 0.7  
C3. No spillovers / SUTVA ......................... 0.6  
C4. Exogeneity of treatment timing ................ 0.7  
C5. Correct inference (clustering, heterogeneity).. 1.0  

Overall, the design is credible but hinges on successfully demonstrating common trends and containing spillovers.
